summary: This informational document defines the role of the operators of IETF protocol parameter registries, which record values that protocols use, so those values mean the same thing everywhere. It describes what such operators do and how they relate to the IETF. It was replaced by RFC 8722.

eli5.summary: Protocols share lists of agreed numbers and names. This says what the people who keep those lists must do. It was later replaced by RFC 8722.

questions: what is a protocol parameter registry operator
role of iana in ietf registries
subtitle: How IETF entrusts the management of shared code point registries.

tldr.problem: IETF protocols use shared number spaces (ports, algorithms, message types). These registries must be centrally managed so the same number always means the same thing everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF separates policy-making from day-to-day registry management, appointing a Registry Operator under IAB oversight to maintain the registries, process assignments, and report on performance.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 8722, which updates the roles and requirements in light of changes to IETF administration.

facts.label: Allocation policies
facts.value: First Come First Served, Expert Review, Standards Action

today: RFC 8722 replaces RFC 6220. It updates the roles of IETF bodies involved in registry management to reflect changes to IETF administration after the transition away from the IAOC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IETF protocols often need to use specific numbers or codes that must be the same everywhere. For example, a protocol might define that code 1 means "REQUEST" and code 2 means "REPLY". To ensure every implementation understands these values the same way, the IETF maintains protocol parameter registries—central records that assign and document what each value means.

This RFC describes how the IETF manages this function. It defines the roles of various IETF bodies in overseeing registries and the responsibilities of whoever is appointed to run them—the Protocol Parameter Registry Operator, traditionally called the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) function.
sections.eli5: Protocols share numbers like "17 means UDP" or "80 means web traffic". Someone has to keep the official list of what every number means and make sure new ones don't conflict. This document says how that job works.

sections.title: Registries and the Registry Operator
sections.content:
A protocol parameter registry records the valid values for a specific protocol parameter and what each value means. Each registry is controlled by a set of rules (an allocation policy) that determines who can request a new assignment and how it is reviewed. A protocol might specify that some values use a "First Come, First Served" policy (quick assignment, no review) while others require "Expert Review" (an expert checks that the proposed value makes sense).

The Registry Operator implements these policies on behalf of the IETF. It reviews requests, checks them against the rules, maintains the registries as public databases, and publishes them online. The Operator also advises the IESG on whether new RFC specifications have clear IANA instructions.
sections.eli5: The Registry Operator is the person or organization that keeps the official list, adds new entries when asked, and publishes it for everyone to see.

sections.title: The Organizational Framework
sections.content:
The IETF delegates this function to keep a healthy separation of concerns. The IAB (Internet Architecture Board) sets policy—it defines what registries exist and appoints the Operator. The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) provides technical direction: when an RFC requests a registry or an assignment, the IESG ensures the request is clear and consistent with IETF guidelines. The IETF Trust holds the copyright and intellectual property rights to all registry contents, ensuring they remain public and free.

The IAOC (IETF Administrative Oversight Committee) identifies vendors to be the Registry Operator and manages the contract with them. This structural separation prevents a single body from both setting the rules and making individual allocation decisions, reducing conflicts of interest.
sections.eli5: Different IETF groups do different jobs: one makes the rules, one checks that requests make sense, one holds the copyright, and one hires and manages the actual registry operator company.

sections.title: Operator Responsibilities
sections.content:
The RFC enumerates the duties of the Registry Operator. These include: reviewing new RFCs to advise on their IANA sections; maintaining and publishing the registries publicly and free of charge; processing assignment requests according to the allocation policy for each registry; maintaining mailing lists for expert reviews; appointing a liaison contact for the IESG; reporting performance metrics to the IAB; and ensuring all registry contents are published and redistributable.

When the RFC is unclear or there is a technical dispute, the Operator defers to the IESG for guidance. The Operator also works with the IETF to develop missing criteria over time and adopts them when instructed by the IESG.
sections.eli5: The operator keeps the registries running every day, adds new entries, publishes them free online, and reports to the IETF on how things are going.

sections.title: Status and Successor
sections.content: RFC 6220 was published in April 2011 and served as the foundational description of IETF registry operator roles for a decade. In 2020, RFC 8722 was published to update these roles in light of structural changes to IETF administration, particularly the transition away from the IAOC. RFC 6220 is marked Informational and is now obsoleted by RFC 8722, which supersedes its requirements.
sections.eli5: This document described the job until 2020, when RFC 8722 updated the rules to match how the IETF is run today.
